ChatGPT said:

Here’s the key point:

Your 2004A (20×4) LCD uses the exact same controller (HD44780 or compatible) as 1602 (16×2) displays.
There is no such thing as a special “4-line initialization command.”
You must use the standard 2-line, 8-bit initialization sequence.

✔ The Good News

Your Initialize_2Line_LCD() is correct.
Your Initialize_4Line_LCD() is wrong — it is just a copy of the 2-line version and does nothing special.

✔ Why?

A 20×4 LCD is internally wired as two 20×2 LCDs.
The HD44780 controller only supports 1-line or 2-line modes.
So for ANY 20×4 LCD:

pgsql
Function set is ALWAYS 0x38  (8-bit, 2-line, 5×8)

Nothing else is needed.

✅ What you must change

1. Use Initialize_2Line_LCD() instead of Initialize_4Line_LCD()

In your main():

c
LCD_init();
ToggleEnablePin();
Initialize_2Line_LCD();

Delete or ignore Initialize_4Line_LCD().

2. Fix writing data

When writing characters, use:

c
SendDataToLCD('H');
SendDataToLCD('e');
SendDataToLCD('l');
SendDataToLCD('l');
SendDataToLCD('o');

Right now you are calling:

c
SendCharachterToTheLCDDataPins()

This writes the bits but does not set RS=1.
So the LCD sees them as commands, not characters.

3. Make sure RW is always LOW (Write mode)

You never set RW low.
Add this after configuring GPIO:

c
SendBitToPortAndPin(RW_Port, RW_Pin, 0);

Otherwise the LCD may be stuck in read mode.

4. Double-check your pin wiring

Your definitions:

ini
D0 = PB10  
D1 = PB11  
D2 = PB12  
D3 = PB13  
D4 = PB14  
D5 = PB15  
D6 = PB5  
D7 = PB6  
RS = PB8  
RW = PB9  
EN = PC15

Make sure your physical wiring matches these unusual mappings.

5. Enable pulse timing is extremely small

You use:

c
for(volatile int i = 0; i < 1000; i++);

At 72 MHz, this is ~15–20 µs.
LCD spec requires >450 ns, so your delay is OK.

✔ The correct workflow for a 20×4 LCD

c
LCD_init();

SendBitToPortAndPin(RW_Port, RW_Pin, 0); // Always write

Initialize_2Line_LCD();  // correct for all HD44780 20×4

SendDataToLCD('H');
SendDataToLCD('e');
SendDataToLCD('l');
SendDataToLCD('l');
SendDataToLCD('o');

⭐ OPTIONAL (important): Implement "go to line" commands

20×4 LCDs have unusual DDRAM addresses:

LineDDRAM address
10x00
20x40
30x14
40x54

Example:

c
void LCD_SetCursor(uint8_t row, uint8_t col)
{
    const uint8_t row_offsets[4] = {0x00, 0x40, 0x14, 0x54};
    SendCommandToLCD(0x80 | (row_offsets[row] + col));
}

✔ Final summary (do these 4 things)

1. Use Initialize_2Line_LCD()

20×4 LCDs internally use “2-line” mode.

2. Replace your character writes with SendDataToLCD()

Otherwise RS is wrong.

3. Set RW = 0

Required for write mode.

4. Verify wiring

Your pin mapping is non-standard.

If you want, paste your wiring diagram and I'll verify every pin.

ChatGPT said:

You’re very close, but the error you’re seeing:

vbnet
undefined reference to `sprintf'

has nothing to do with your LCD code — it is a linker error.

✅ Why this happens

sprintf() is part of the standard C library, but:

🛑 Newlib-nano does NOT include sprintf() by default

Most STM32 projects (CubeIDE, makefile templates, bare-metal setups) link against:

diff
-lc -lnosys -u _printf_float

But newlib-nano removes many functions, including sprintf(), unless you ask for them.

Result:

👉 Compiler knows sprintf() exists (because you #include <stdio.h>),
👉 but the linker cannot find it, so it throws:

css
undefined reference to sprintf

✅ How to fix it

You have 3 options — choose the one you prefer.

OPTION 1 (Recommended): Enable full stdio support

Add this flag to your linker flags:

diff
-u _printf_float

and change:

ini
-specs=nano.specs

to

ini
-specs=nosys.specs

This links the full version of sprintf().

OPTION 2: Keep nano library but enable formatted I/O

Append this to your linker command:

diff
-u _printf_float -u _scanf_float

Or simpler:

diff
-Wl,-u,_printf_float

OPTION 3 (Best for small MCUs): Replace sprintf with your own tiny integer-to-string function

This avoids linking the entire stdio library (saves ~10 KB!).

Example:

c
void int_to_string(int value, char *buffer)
{
    char temp[12];
    int i = 0, j = 0;

    if (value < 0) {
        buffer[j++] = '-';
        value = -value;
    }

    do {
        temp[i++] = (value % 10) + '0';
        value /= 10;
    } while (value);

    while (i--) {
        buffer[j++] = temp[i];
    }

    buffer[j] = '\0';
}

Usage:

c
char buf[12];
int_to_string(200, buf);
LCDSendAString(buf);

Much leaner, no linker problems.

⚠️ Additional Important Fixes in Your LCD Code

While reviewing your updated code, I noticed two issues you must fix.

❗ PROBLEM 1 — RW pin is never initialized

You commented this out:

c
// SendBitToPortAndPin(RW_Port, RW_Pin, 0);  // always write

RW should always be 0.

Place this in LCD_init() at the end:

c
SendBitToPortAndPin(RW_Port, RW_Pin, 0);

❗ PROBLEM 2 — Calling SendCommandToLCD(0xC0) twice

You do:

c
SendCommandToLCD(0xC0); // Move cursor to line 2
LCDSendAString("STM32 LCD Test");

char StringNumber[10];
sprintf...

SendCommandToLCD(0xC0); // AGAIN send command for line 2
LCDSendAString(StringNumber);

→ This overwrites what you just printed.

You probably meant:

c
SendCommandToLCD(0x80 | 0x14); // Go to 3rd line

For a 20×4 LCD, DDRAM addresses are:

LineDDRAM Start
10x00
20x40
30x14
40x54

📌 Final Answer Summary

✔ To fix the linker error:

Enable full stdio or avoid sprintf.

✔ To fix LCD problems:

  1. Set RW = 0 always

  2. Fix cursor positioning

  3. Use InitializeLCD() only (2-line mode)

  4. Use SendDataToLCD(), not raw bit writes

If you want, I can look at your Makefile and tell you exactly what line to change for enabling sprintf.

ChatGPT said:

Your makefile is not linking the standard C library at all, so sprintf() cannot be resolved.

Right now your link command is:

css
arm-none-eabi-gcc  -nostdlib  <objects>  ...

-nostdlib = do NOT link libc, do NOT link libgcc, do NOT link newlib
→ ✔ This is why sprintf() is undefined.

You must link the standard C library.

✅ Minimal fix (recommended)

Remove -nostdlib and explicitly link:

  • -lc → Standard C library

  • -lm → Math library (newlib sometimes needs it)

  • -lgcc → GCC support library

  • -lnosys → Syscall stubs for bare-metal

  • --specs=nano.specs (optional): smaller newlib

🔧 Fix your linker flags

Modify this line:

make
LFLAGS = -nostdlib -T startup_linker/stm32F103_linker_script.ld -Wl,-Map=bin/LCD_8bit.map

to:

make
LFLAGS = -T startup_linker/stm32F103_linker_script.ld \
         -Wl,-Map=bin/LCD_8bit.map \
         --specs=nano.specs \
         -lc -lm -lnosys -lgcc

🔧 Your final link rule should be:

make
LCD_8bit.elf : $(OFILES)
	$(CC) $(LFLAGS)  build/stm32f103_startup.o build/LCD.o build/kernel.o -o bin/LCD_8bit.elf

🧪 If you want full sprintf (with floats), add:

diff
-Wl,-u,_printf_float

So the full flags become:

make
LFLAGS = -T startup_linker/stm32F103_linker_script.ld \
         -Wl,-Map=bin/LCD_8bit.map \
         --specs=nano.specs \
         -Wl,-u,_printf_float \
         -lc -lm -lnosys -lgcc

🎉 That’s it!

After this change, your project will finally link sprintf() correctly.

If you want, paste your updated makefile, and I will confirm it’s 100% correct.

ChatGPT said:

This new error:

vbnet
undefined reference to `end'   (from _sbrk in libnosys)

means:

👉 Your linker script does not define the symbol _end or end,

which newlib's _sbrk() implementation requires.

This is very common when enabling newlib on a custom STM32 bare-metal project.

✅ WHY IT HAPPENS

The default _sbrk() implementation in libnosys.a assumes your linker script defines:

arduino
end

or:

nginx
_end

This marks the start of the heap.

Without it, the linker fails.

✅ THE FIX

You must add _end (or end) to your linker script.

Find your linker script:

bash
startup_linker/stm32F103_linker_script.ld

Inside the .bss or RAM section, add:

ld
/* End of global variables — start of heap */
_end = .;
PROVIDE(end = .);

📌 Where exactly should it go?

Here is a typical STM32F1 linker script structure:

ld
SECTIONS
{
    .text :

This ensures newlib has a valid heap starting address.

🎯 Alternative: provide your own _sbrk() implementation

This avoids using libnosys.

Add this to a new file syscalls.c:

c
#include <sys/types.h>
extern char _end;   // Defined in linker script
static char *heap_end;

caddr_t _sbrk(int incr)
{
    if (heap_end == 0)
        heap_end = &_end;

    char *prev = heap_end;
    heap_end += incr;
    return (caddr_t)prev;
}

This is what most bare-metal STM32 projects do.

_end = .;
PROVIDE(end = .);

inside .bss.

No need to modify anything else.

Great — your linker script is clear, and the fix is simple.

The problem is that you have not defined _end or end, which newlib-nano requires for _sbrk() (heap allocation).

You need to define _end at the end of your .bss section.

✅ Fix: Add _end and end inside your .bss section

Modify your .bss section like this:

ld
/*third section of output file*/
.bss :
{
    . = ALIGN(4);
    _sbss = .;          /*start of bss*/
    *(.bss)
    . = ALIGN(4);
    _ebss = .;          /*end of bss*/

    /* >>> ADD THESE TWO LINES <<< */
    _end = .;
    PROVIDE(end = .);

} > SRAM

🧠 Why this fixes the problem

  • _end marks the first free RAM address after .bss.

  • Newlib-nano’s _sbrk() uses this as the start of the heap.

  • Without _end, you get:

vbnet
undefined reference to `end'

because libnosys.a tries to reference it.

✔ After adding this

Your project will link successfully
AND
sprintf() (and other libc functions) will have a valid heap region.

🔧 Optional improvement: define _heap_start and _heap_end

Not required, but nice to have:

_heap_start = _end;
_heap_end   = ORIGIN(SRAM) + LENGTH(SRAM) - __max_stack_size;

But again — this is optional.

Great — your startup code is good, and it clearly shows the problem:

✅ Your startup code uses these symbols:

c
extern uint32_t _sbss;
extern uint32_t _ebss;
extern uint32_t _sdata;
extern uint32_t _edata;
extern uint32_t _etext;

✔ All of these are correctly defined in your linker script.
❌ BUT the newlib library you linked (libnosys.a) also expects:

markdown
__bss_start__
__bss_end__

which your linker script does NOT define, causing:

vbnet
undefined reference to `__bss_start__'
undefined reference to `__bss_end__'

✅ The correct fix is in the linker script — NOT in the startup code

Your startup code already uses your _sbss and _ebss symbols, and those are perfectly fine.

You simply need to export additional aliases so that the standard library can find the expected symbols.

✅ FIX — Add these four lines to your linker script inside .bss:

ld
__bss_start__ = _sbss;
__bss_end__   = _ebss;
PROVIDE(__bss_start__ = _sbss);
PROVIDE(__bss_end__   = _ebss);

Here is exactly how your .bss section should look:

ld
.bss :
{
    . = ALIGN(4);
    _sbss = .;
    *(.bss)
    . = ALIGN(4);
    _ebss = .;

    /* required by newlib / libnosys */
    _end = .;
    PROVIDE(end = .);

    /* required by libraries expecting __bss_start__ and __bss_end__ */
    __bss_start__ = _sbss;
    __bss_end__   = _ebss;
    PROVIDE(__bss_start__ = _sbss);
    PROVIDE(__bss_end__   = _ebss);

} > SRAM

This satisfies:

  • your startup file (_sbss, _ebss)

  • newlib (__bss_start__, __bss_end__)

  • _sbrk() heap (_end, end)

⚠ IMPORTANT NOTE

Your startup code has a bug in data copying:

c
uint32_t *p_dest_mem = (uint32_t *)&_edata;

This is wrong — it should point to _sdata, the beginning of the RAM .data section.

Correct version:

c
uint32_t *p_dest_mem = (uint32_t *)&_sdata;

Otherwise nothing gets copied into RAM correctly.

ALSO your loop is wrong:

c
for(uint32_t i =0; i < data_mem_size; i++)

This copies bytes, but your pointers are uint32_t, so you skip bytes and miscopy memory.

Correct version:

c
uint32_t data_mem_words = data_mem_size / 4;

for(uint32_t i = 0; i < data_mem_words; i++) {
    *p_dest_mem++ = *p_src_mem++;
}

__bss_end__   = _ebss;
PROVIDE(__bss_start__ = _sbss);
PROVIDE(__bss_end__   = _ebss);

Replace:

c
uint32_t *p_dest_mem = (uint32_t *)&_edata;
for(uint32_t i =0; i < data_mem_size; i++)

With:

c
uint32_t *p_dest_mem = (uint32_t *)&_sdata;
uint32_t data_mem_words = data_mem_size / 4;

#include <sys/stat.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int _close(int file) { return -1; }
int _fstat(int file, struct stat *st)
{
    st->st_mode = S_IFCHR;
    return 0;
}
int _isatty(int file) { return 1; }
int _lseek(int file, int ptr, int dir) { return 0; }
int _read(int file, char *ptr, int len) { return 0; }

// Redirect printf output to nothing
int _write(int file, char *ptr, int len)
{
    return len; // pretend everything was written
}

// Newlib needs a heap pointer
extern char _end;
static char *heap_end;
caddr_t _sbrk(int incr)
{
    if (heap_end == 0)
        heap_end = &_end;

    char *prev = heap_end;
    heap_end += incr;
    return (caddr_t)prev;
}

This removes the warnings and makes newlib happy.

SendCommandToLCD(0x30); delay(5);

        SendDataToLCD(*str++);
        delay_us(50); // small delay after each character

4️⃣ Initialize LCD properly

Your current InitializeLCD() may not support 4-line LCDs correctly. Use the standard sequence for HD44780 20×4:

c
void InitializeLCD(void) {
    delay_ms(40);  // wait after power-up

    SendCommandToLCD(0x30);
    delay_ms(5);

    SendCommandToLCD(0x30);
    delay_ms(1);

    SendCommandToLCD(0x30);
    delay_ms(1);

    SendCommandToLCD(0x38); // 8-bit, 2-line (works for 4-line 20x4)
    SendCommandToLCD(0x0C); // Display ON, Cursor OFF
    SendCommandToLCD(0x01); // Clear display
    delay_ms(2);
    SendCommandToLCD(0x06); // Entry mode: increment cursor

The LCD needs some microseconds or milliseconds to process commands. For example, after:

You must wait ~2ms, otherwise the next write will be ignored.

SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD1Port, LCDD1Pin, (character >> 1) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD2Port, LCDD2Pin, (character >> 2) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD3Port, LCDD3Pin, (character >> 3) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD4Port, LCDD4Pin, (character >> 4) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD5Port, LCDD5Pin, (character >> 5) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD6Port, LCDD6Pin, (character >> 6) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD7Port, LCDD7Pin, (character >> 7) & 1);

Ah! Now I see exactly why lines 3 & 4 aren’t displaying anything on your 20×4 LCD. This is a classic HD44780 “4-line LCD quirk” issue combined with a bitmask problem in your driver. Let me explain clearly.

1️⃣ Bitmask issue in SendCharachterToTheLCDDataPins()

You currently have:

c
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD1Port, LCDD1Pin, character & 0b00000010);

  • character & 0b00000010 gives 0 or 2, not 0 or 1.

  • SendBitToPortAndPin() expects 0 or 1, not 2.

  • This means some pins will be treated as always HIGH, breaking character display.

Fix: shift the bit before sending:

c
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD0Port, LCDD0Pin, (character >> 0) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD1Port, LCDD1Pin, (character >> 1) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD2Port, LCDD2Pin, (character >> 2) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD3Port, LCDD3Pin, (character >> 3) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD4Port, LCDD4Pin, (character >> 4) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD5Port, LCDD5Pin, (character >> 5) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD6Port, LCDD6Pin, (character >> 6) & 1);
SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD7Port, LCDD7Pin, (character >> 7) & 1);

✅ This alone can fix a lot of display glitches, including missing characters.

2️⃣ 20×4 LCD addressing

HD44780 20×4 LCD does NOT have 4 continuous lines in memory:

LCD LineDDRAM Address
10x00 → send 0x80
20x40 → send 0xC0
30x14 → send 0x94
40x54 → send 0xD4

  • You used 0x94 for line 3 ✅

  • You used 0xD4 for line 4 ✅

  • These are correct, but they will only work if the LCD is properly initialized.

3️⃣ Initialization for 4-line LCD

Your current InitializeLCD() sends:

c
SendCommandToLCD(0x38); // 8-bit, 2-line, 5x8 dots

  • Problem: you told it “2-line mode”, not 4-line mode.

  • HD44780 maps 20×4 internally as 2 sets of 2 lines, so 0x38 works, but sometimes line 3 & 4 don’t update correctly without a delay after line 2.

Add small delays after each SendCommandToLCD(), especially after clearing display or moving cursor:

c
SendCommandToLCD(0x01); // Clear display
for(volatile int i=0;i<50000;i++); // wait >1.6ms

SendCommandToLCD(0x80); // Move cursor to line 1
for(volatile int i=0;i<20000;i++); // wait

4️⃣ SendCommand and SendData delays

Your SendDataToLCD() has a small delay, but SendCommandToLCD() does not:

c
void SendCommandToLCD(uint8_t command)
{
    SendBitToPortAndPin(RS_Port, RS_Pin, 0);
    SendCharachterToTheLCDDataPins(command);
    ToggleEnablePin();
    for(volatile int i=0;i<2000;i++); // add small delay
}

  • Without this delay, cursor moves may be ignored by LCD for line 3 & 4.

✅ Summary of fixes

  1. Correct bitmasking in SendCharachterToTheLCDDataPins() (shift & mask).

  2. Add small delays after each command in SendCommandToLCD() and after clearing display.

  3. Use correct DDRAM addresses (0x80, 0xC0, 0x94, 0xD4) — you already did this.

  4. Optional: implement LCD_GotoXY(x,y) so you don’t have to memorize DDRAM addresses.

5️⃣ Example: Corrected SendCharachterToTheLCDDataPins()

c
void SendCharachterToTheLCDDataPins(char character)
{
    SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD0Port, LCDD0Pin, (character >> 0) & 1);
    SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD1Port, LCDD1Pin, (character >> 1) & 1);
    SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD2Port, LCDD2Pin, (character >> 2) & 1);
    SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD3Port, LCDD3Pin, (character >> 3) & 1);
    SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD4Port, LCDD4Pin, (character >> 4) & 1);
    SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD5Port, LCDD5Pin, (character >> 5) & 1);
    SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD6Port, LCDD6Pin, (character >> 6) & 1);
    SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD7Port, LCDD7Pin, (character >> 7) & 1);
}

After this fix and small delays in SendCommandToLCD(), your lines 3 & 4 should display properly.

✅ THE REAL PROBLEM: Your InitializeLCD() is EMPTY!

You posted:

…but there is NO CODE inside it !

That means:

  • No function set

  • No display on

  • No clear display

  • No entry mode

  • No initialization sequence at all

Your LCD is never initialized.

Yet you're calling line addressing commands:

c

SendCommandToLCD(0xD4); // line 4

The LCD will ignore all these commands if initialization never occurred.

🔥 You MUST put back the initialization sequence:

Here is a correct, working InitializeLCD() for 20x4 LCD, 8-bit mode:

c
void InitializeLCD(void)
{
    // Wait >40ms after power up
    for (volatile int i = 0; i < 50000; i++);

    // Initialization sequence (8-bit mode)
    SendCommandToLCD(0x30);
    for (volatile int i = 0; i < 10000; i++);

    SendCommandToLCD(0x30);
    for (volatile int i = 0; i < 10000; i++);

    SendCommandToLCD(0x30);
    for (volatile int i = 0; i < 10000; i++);

    // Function set: 8-bit, 2 lines, 5x8 font
    SendCommandToLCD(0x38);

    // Display ON, cursor off
    SendCommandToLCD(0x0C);

    // Clear display
    SendCommandToLCD(0x01);
    for (volatile int i = 0; i < 50000; i++);

    // Entry mode: increment, no shift
    SendCommandToLCD(0x06);
}

❗ WHY LINES 1 & 2 WORKED BUT 3 & 4 DIDN’T

Lines 1 & 2 sometimes work because the LCD powers-up in a semi-random state that sometimes accepts ASCII writes…

…but it will not accept DDRAM address commands (0x94, 0xD4) unless it is fully initialized.

So only line 1/2 appear (by chance), and lines 3/4 ALWAYS fail.

void InitializeLCD(void)
{
    // Wait >40ms after power rises above 2.7V
    for (volatile int i = 0; i < 80000; i++);

    // 8-bit init sequence required by HD44780
    SendCommandToLCD(0x30);
    for (volatile int i = 0; i < 80000; i++);

    SendCommandToLCD(0x30);
    for (volatile int i = 0; i < 20000; i++);

    SendCommandToLCD(0x30);
    for (volatile int i = 0; i < 20000; i++);

    // Now the LCD is ready for real config
    SendCommandToLCD(0x38);  // 8-bit, 2-line, 5x8 font
    SendCommandToLCD(0x0C);  // Display ON, no cursor
    SendCommandToLCD(0x01);  // Clear display
    for (volatile int i = 0; i < 50000; i++);

    SendCommandToLCD(0x06);  // Entry mode
}

This is the official HD44780 power-on initialization sequence for 8-bit mode and works on every 20×4 LCD.

1️⃣ 20×4 LCD DDRAM Layout

Most 20×4 HD44780-based LCDs do NOT have a contiguous 0x00–0x27 address for all 4 lines. The actual DDRAM addresses are usually:

LineDDRAM Address
10x00–0x13
20x40–0x53
30x14–0x27
40x54–0x67

This is why simply sending 0x94 and 0xD4 does not go to lines 3 and 4 on many 20×4 LCDs.

2️⃣ Correct DDRAM addresses for 20×4 LCD

For a 20×4 LCD (HD44780 standard), the DDRAM addresses for first character of each line are:

c
#define LINE1_ADDR 0x00
#define LINE2_ADDR 0x40
#define LINE3_ADDR 0x14
#define LINE4_ADDR 0x54

To move the cursor, you must send:

c

SendCommandToLCD(0x80 | LINE2_ADDR);
SendCommandToLCD(0x80 | LINE3_ADDR);
SendCommandToLCD(0x80 | LINE4_ADDR);

Notice the 0x80 | part — it is required by the HD44780 command set. Without it, the LCD thinks you are sending a raw command, not a DDRAM address.

#define LINE2_ADDR 0x40
#define LINE3_ADDR 0x14

void LCDGotoLine(uint8_t line)
{

    {

        case 3: SendCommandToLCD(0x80 | LINE3_ADDR); break;
        case 4: SendCommandToLCD(0x80 | LINE4_ADDR); break;
        default: break;
    }
}

Here’s the correct DDRAM mapping for 20×4:

LineDDRAM Address Start
10x00

30x14
40x54

Your code tries 0x94 and 0xD4, which is wrong for a standard 20×4. That’s why line 4 is blank.

void LCDGotoXY(uint8_t line, uint8_t column)
{
    uint8_t address;
    switch(line)
    {
        case 1: address = 0x00; break;
        case 2: address = 0x40; break;
        case 3: address = 0x14; break;
        case 4: address = 0x54; break;
        default: address = 0x00; break;
    }
    SendCommandToLCD(0x80 | (address + column - 1));
}

#include "stm32f103xb.h"

#include "LCD.h"

// Pin and port configurations for LCD data pins and control pins

#define LCDD0Pin 10

#define LCDD0Port GPIOB

#define LCDD1Pin 11

#define LCDD1Port GPIOB

#define LCDD2Pin 12

#define LCDD2Port GPIOB

#define LCDD3Pin 13

#define LCDD3Port GPIOB

#define LCDD4Pin 14

#define LCDD4Port GPIOB

#define LCDD5Pin 15

#define LCDD5Port GPIOB

#define LCDD6Pin 5

#define LCDD6Port GPIOB

#define LCDD7Pin 6

#define LCDD7Port GPIOB

#define RS_Pin 8

#define RS_Port GPIOB

#define RW_Pin 9

#define RW_Port GPIOB

#define Enable_Pin 15

#define Enable_Port GPIOC

// INitialize GPIO Ports for LCD

void LCD_init(void)

{

// USING RCC TO ENABLE CLOCK FOR PORT B AND PORT C

RCC->APB2ENR |= (1U << 4); // Enable clock to port c

RCC->APB2ENR |= (1U << 3); // Enable clock to port B

// USING GPIO TO SET THE PINS AS OUTPUT

// Set Mode and CNF of pin PC15 to output max speed 50Mhz

GPIOC->CRH |= (1 << 28); // PC15

GPIOC->CRH |= (1 << 29); // PC15

GPIOC->CRH &= ~(1 << 30); // PC15

GPIOC->CRH &= ~(1 << 31); // PC15

// uSING GPIO TO SET THE PINS AS OUTPUT

// Set Mode and CNF of pin PB5,PB6,PB8,PB9,PB10,PB12,PB13,PB14,PB15 to output max speed

GPIOB->CRL |= (1 << 20); // PB5

GPIOB->CRL |= (1 << 21); // PB5

GPIOB->CRL &= ~(1 << 22); // PB5

GPIOB->CRL &= ~(1 << 23); // PB5

GPIOB->CRL |= (1 << 24); // PB6

GPIOB->CRL |= (1 << 25); // PB6

GPIOB->CRL &= ~(1 << 26); // PB6

GPIOB->CRL &= ~(1 << 27); // PB6

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 0); // PB8

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 1); // PB8

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 2); // PB8

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 3); // PB8

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 4); // PB9

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 5); // PB9

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 6); // PB9

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 7); // PB9

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 8); // PB10

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 9); // PB10

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 10); // PB10

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 11); // PB10

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 12); // PB11

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 13); // PB11

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 14); // PB11

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 15); // PB11

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 16); // PB12

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 17); // PB12

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 18); // PB12

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 19); // PB12

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 20); // PB13

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 21); // PB13

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 22); // PB13

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 23); // PB13

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 24); // PB14

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 25); // PB14

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 26); // PB14

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 27); // PB14

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 28); // PB15

GPIOB->CRH |= (1 << 29); // PB15

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 30); // PB15

GPIOB->CRH &= ~(1 << 31); // PB15

/* // Alternative way of setting the pins as output Curious!!!!

GPIOC->CRH &= ~0x0FF00000; // Clear PC15 bits

GPIOC->CRH |= 0x03300000; // PC15 as output max speed 50Mhz

GPIOC->CRL &= ~0x0FF00000; // Clear PB5,PB6 bits

GPIOB->CRL |= 0x03300000; // PB5,PB6 as output max speed 50Mhz

GPIOB->CRH &= ~0xFFFFFFFF; // Clear PB8,PB9,PB10,PB11,PB12,PB13,PB14,PB15 bits

GPIOB->CRH |= 0x33333333; // PB8,PB9,PB10,PB11,PB12,PB13,PB14,PB15 as output max speed 50Mhz

*/

// SendBitToPortAndPin(RW_Port, RW_Pin, 0); // always write

}

void SendBitToPortAndPin(GPIO_TypeDef *port, int pinNumber, uint8_t bitState)

// hover over GPIOB with your mouse you will see it is a TypeDef struct pointer so we use GPIO_TypeDef * and port represents the port

{

if (bitState)

{

port->BSRR |= (1U << pinNumber); // Set pin

}

else

{

port->BRR |= (1U << pinNumber); // Reset pin

}

}

void SendCharachterToTheLCDDataPins(char character)

{

SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD0Port, LCDD0Pin, (character >> 0) & 1);

SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD1Port, LCDD1Pin, (character >> 1) & 1);

SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD2Port, LCDD2Pin, (character >> 2) & 1);

SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD3Port, LCDD3Pin, (character >> 3) & 1);

SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD4Port, LCDD4Pin, (character >> 4) & 1);

SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD5Port, LCDD5Pin, (character >> 5) & 1);

SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD6Port, LCDD6Pin, (character >> 6) & 1);

SendBitToPortAndPin(LCDD7Port, LCDD7Pin, (character >> 7) & 1);

}

void ToggleEnablePin()

{

SendBitToPortAndPin(Enable_Port, Enable_Pin, 1);

for (volatile int i = 0; i < 1000; i++)

;

SendBitToPortAndPin(Enable_Port, Enable_Pin, 0);

for (volatile int i = 0; i < 1000; i++)

;

}

void SendCommandToLCD(uint8_t command)

{

SendBitToPortAndPin(RS_Port, RS_Pin, 0); // RS = 0 for command

for (volatile int i = 0; i < 2000; i++)

; // Small delay

SendBitToPortAndPin(RW_Port, RW_Pin, 0); // RW = 0 for write

for (volatile int i = 0; i < 2000; i++)

; // Small delay

SendCharachterToTheLCDDataPins(command);

for (volatile int i = 0; i < 2000; i++)

; // Small delay

ToggleEnablePin();

}

void SendDataToLCD(uint8_t data)

{

SendBitToPortAndPin(RS_Port, RS_Pin, 1); // RS = 1 for data

SendBitToPortAndPin(RW_Port, RW_Pin, 0); // RW = 0 for write

SendCharachterToTheLCDDataPins(data);

ToggleEnablePin();

for (volatile int i = 0; i < 2000; i++)

; //

}

void LCDSendAString(const char *StringOfCharachters)

{

while (*StringOfCharachters != '\0')

{

SendDataToLCD((uint8_t)(*StringOfCharachters));

StringOfCharachters++;

}

}

void InitializeLCD(void)

{

// Wait >40ms after power rises above 2.7V

for (volatile int i = 0; i < 80000; i++)

;

// 8-bit init sequence required by HD44780

SendCommandToLCD(0x30);

for (volatile int i = 0; i < 80000; i++)

;

SendCommandToLCD(0x30);

for (volatile int i = 0; i < 20000; i++)

;

SendCommandToLCD(0x30);

for (volatile int i = 0; i < 20000; i++)

;

// Now the LCD is ready for real config

SendCommandToLCD(0x38); // 8-bit, 2-line, 5x8 font

SendCommandToLCD(0x0C); // Display ON, no cursor

SendCommandToLCD(0x01); // Clear display

for (volatile int i = 0; i < 50000; i++)

;

SendCommandToLCD(0x06); // Entry mode

}

void LCDGotoXY(uint8_t line, uint8_t column)

{

uint8_t address;

switch (line)

{

case 1:

address = 0x00;

break;

case 2:

address = 0x40;

break;

case 3:

address = 0x14;

break;

case 4:

address = 0x54;

break;

default:

address = 0x00;

break;

}

SendCommandToLCD(0x80 | (address + column - 1));

}
